news.Title: Morgan Stanley just made a bold call on Amazon stock
news.Content:
Amazon stock jumped to lead the Dow Jones Industrial Average on Oct. 19, the same day Morgan Stanley named it the firm's top pick and set a price target that would push AWS' total revenue to $1 trillion for the first time, according to Investopedia . Analyst Brian Nowak set a new target of $350, up from $335, representing roughly 40% upside from the stock's Oct. 16 close.

The upgrade lands at an unusual moment. Amazon's cloud business is expanding at a pace Wall Street did not expect. Its AI infrastructure bet is producing visible returns, and one of the company's biggest competitors just ran into a public fight with Amazon over how AI agents shop online. The stars, in Nowak's view, are lining up.

The "Rule of 90" case for buying Amazon now

Nowak's note centers on what he calls the "Rule of 90" for Amazon Web Services. The idea is that when revenue growth plus operating margin crosses 90%, a cloud business earns a premium multiple, Motley Fool reported .

AWS is not there yet, but Nowak thinks it will get there. He projects AWS growth of 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, with operating margins of 42% and 44%, respectively.

Also read: JPMorgan's CEO sends a stern warning to corporate America

Put those numbers together and you get an AWS business that nearly triples its revenue between 2025 and 2028. At those margins, AWS would clear the Rule of 90 threshold and, in Nowak's model, justify a higher valuation for the entire company. He sees Amazon earning around $16.50 a share in 2028, roughly 7% above the Wall Street consensus.

The projection rests on Amazon's position inside the cloud arms race. AWS grew 37% to $42.2 billion in revenue during the second quarter of 2026, its fastest pace in 18 quarters, and is now running at a $169 billion annualized rate. Amazon also raised its 2026 capital expenditure to $220 billion. CEO Andy Jassy cited falling memory prices as one reason to accelerate the spending.

AWS is betting on Bedrock and Nvidia to pull ahead

Nowak's optimism on margins ties directly to Amazon's AI platform strategy. Bedrock, AWS's managed AI service, gives enterprise customers access to at least 10 fully managed third-party models, according to Amazon's SEC filing . Nowak expects Bedrock to become a growing source of high-margin revenue as more companies run their AI workloads on AWS rather than building their own infrastructure.

The hardware picture adds to that argument. AWS and Nvidia announced in August that they would deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia GPUs over roughly the next two years, a commitment that would give AWS one of the largest GPU fleets in the world. That kind of scale matters because the biggest enterprise AI workloads require consistent, massive compute that only a handful of providers can guarantee.

Story Continues

KeyBanc Capital Markets also has a $350 target on Amazon, projecting 38% AWS growth versus a 37% street consensus, as TheStreet reported . Both firms see AWS's trajectory as underappreciated by the broader market.

Meta's Muse just handed Amazon an unexpected edge

One of the more unusual factors in Amazon's favor right now is a fight it did not start. Meta launched Muse, an AI shopping assistant, and integrated it with retailers including Walmart and Best Buy. The plan was for Muse to help users browse, compare and buy products across the web, with Meta collecting a transaction fee on each purchase, according to TheStreet .

More Amazon:

Amazon is coming for your quick Walmart run

Amazon's Alexa shopping tool faces its first big October test

Amazon pulls a best-selling pain reliever again, and customers need to check their medicine cabinets

Amazon blocked Muse from its store on Sept. 20, after Meta declined its request to remove the bot. Amazon bars outside companies from using automated tools to shop on its site, and its spokesperson said third-party agents like Muse have the same obligations as other apps.

Amazon blocked Muse for a reason. Every AI purchase routed through a Meta checkout is a transaction Amazon loses. Blocking the bot kept that money in-house.

What the $350 target means for investors

Morgan Stanley's Overweight rating and $350 price target are not a guarantee. Amazon traded near $250 around Oct. 16, meaning the stock would need to climb about 40% to reach that level. That kind of move rarely happens in a straight line, and a lot has to go right on AWS growth for Nowak's 2028 earnings estimate to hold.

Rate risk is the one to watch. Amazon has $220 billion earmarked for AI infrastructure, and that bet only pays off if enterprise demand stays strong. A pullback leaves a lot of empty rack space.

AWS is growing faster than any major cloud rival. Bedrock is signing enterprise customers. Amazon shut Muse out rather than share the checkout. Nowak's argument is that none of this is fully priced in yet, and that AWS hits the Rule of 90 before the street expects it to.

news.Title: Alphabet Must Show This on Oct. 28 or the Stock Could Stall
news.Content:
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) reports third-quarter results on Wednesday, Oct. 28, and most of the attention will focus on the usual places. This includes how fast Google Cloud grew, whether Search held up, and what the capital spending number looks like. But one line matters more than any of them right now, and it sits a few pages deeper in the release: operating cash flow.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In the second quarter, Alphabet spent $44.9 billion on property and equipment and generated $39.1 billion in cash from operations. For the first time in recent memory, the company's free cash flow was negative, at $5.9 billion. : https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000066/googexhibit991q22026.htm That is not a rounding error for a business that generated $24 billion in free cash flow just two quarters earlier. Alphabet covered the gap by raising $49.6 billion in stock and $20.3 billion in debt in June. A company that spent a decade buying back shares has started selling them.

Google Cloud is doing its part

The bull case is that this is temporary, and the second-quarter earnings report gave that case real support. Google Cloud revenue grew 82% to $24.8 billion, and more importantly, cloud operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion from $2.8 billion a year earlier. That means cloud is now earning roughly $0.36 in operating profit per dollar of revenue, up from about $0.21. Consolidated operating margin expanded two points to 34%.

That is the chain investors need to see hold: cloud growth becomes cloud margin, cloud margin becomes operating income, and operating income becomes cash. In the second quarter, the first two links worked. The third did not.

Operating cash flow actually fell from $45.8 billion in the first quarter to $39.1 billion, even as operating income rose. Part of that was a nearly $7 billion build in inventory, notable for a company that now sells Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) chip systems through its cloud segment, as well as a jump in receivables. Those figures could reverse. But until they do, Alphabet is funding its artificial intelligence build-out with Wall Street's money, not its own.

What Alphabet needs to show

Management raised full-year capital expenditure guidance to $195 billion to $205 billion on the second-quarter call, up from $180 billion to $190 billion, according to Bloomberg Law. Alphabet generated $185.7 billion in operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months. Read those two numbers together, and the problem is obvious: At the current pace, the company is spending more than it makes, and the equity raise bought it time rather than a solution.

Story Continues

On Oct. 28, the metric to focus on is operating cash flow, and the question is whether it moves back toward the $45 billion to $50 billion range the company produced in late 2025 and early 2026. If it does, the working-capital drag was a blip, the cloud profits are real cash, and the capex budget is self-funding. The stock can keep working. If operating cash flow remains flat or slips again while capex climbs, Alphabet's AI story will be financed by shareholders, and the market will start pricing it that way.

To me, the cloud results have earned Alphabet some patience, and existing shareholders have little reason to sell ahead of the report. But anyone considering a purchase should wait for the cash flow statement, not the press release headline. One quarter of negative free cash flow is a story. Two would be a trend.

news.Title: Prediction: 3 Stocks That Will Be Worth More Than Apple 5 Years From Now
news.Content:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) recently reclaimed the mantle as the world's largest company by market cap, at least for a short while. However, when looking five years out, I think three stocks will be worth more: Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG).

Apple is a great company, with one of the best compounding businesses on the planet. However, the stock currently trades at a very high valuation given its growth prospects, which likely limits its upside over the next five years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

As such, let's see why I think these three growth stocks will surpass it by the end of 2031.

1. SpaceX

With a market cap of about $2 trillion, SpaceX is the smallest company on this list, and its stock will need to deliver some pretty strong returns to overtake Apple, which has a $5 trillion valuation. However, I think a likely merger with Tesla (market cap of $1.5 billion) in the next few years will quickly close the gap.

Barring a merger with Tesla, though, I think SpaceX has the opportunity to grow into a company larger than Apple by 2031, even as a stand-alone company. CEO Elon Musk recently projected that the company will reach $500 billion to $1 trillion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in 2027, led by its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure business. With the company achieving a one-year payback on its chip and networking investments and planning to add a massive 10 to 20 gigawatts of computing power next year, the path to reaching that number is actually quite clear.

Throw in Starship, Starlink, and its Cursor AI coding business, and SpaceX looks poised to see massive revenue growth over the next five years. It looks as if SpaceX could actually crush Musk's $1 trillion 2030 revenue prediction, but even placing a 10-times price-to-sales (P/S) multiple on that would take SpaceX to being a $10 trillion company.

2. Nvidia

With a $5 trillion market cap, Nvidia would only have to outperform Apple over the next five years to be the larger company. Meanwhile, the chipmaker is growing much faster and is trading at less than half the valuation of Apple on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis, at only 13 times fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) analyst estimates.

Story Continues

Nvidia looks poised to remain one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI build-out. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are still the main chips used to train AI models, while it continues to take a larger slice of spending through its networking, central processing units (CPUs), language processing units (LPUs) for inference, and open-weight Nemotron models.

Meanwhile, Nvidia is also set to ride SpaceX's huge AI spending, as the space company ramps up its computing capacity. With SpaceX consolidating on Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture and Nvidia getting roughly $40 billion per gigawatt of power, the company still has huge growth ahead.

3. Alphabet

With a market cap near $4 trillion, Alphabet has some catching up to do to overtake Apple in the next five years, but I'd be very surprised if it doesn't. The company is the most complete AI player and has built-in advantages in distribution and monetization.

Alphabet's biggest edge is that it has taken a wide lead in custom AI chips with its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). This gives it several advantages, starting with its cloud computing unit, where, with its own chips, it gets a payback in about a year, half the time it takes when using Nvidia GPUs. Meanwhile, Anthropic is set to become a major TPU customer, adding another revenue stream for the company.

On top of that, its TPUs allow it to train its AI models and run inference more cheaply than competitors. With Google Search as the gateway to the internet and given Alphabet's ownership of Chrome and Android, as well as a search revenue-sharing deal with Apple, the company also has a major distribution advantage that helps drive usage and growth. Its global ad network also allows it to better monetize the consumer market than upstarts.

As the most profitable company in the world entering this year, just ahead of Nvidia, and with strong growth ahead, Alphabet looks poised to be a bigger company than Apple by 2031.

news.Title: Anthropic's Billions in Microsoft Commitments Add to Its Mounting Compute Bill
news.Content:
Anthropic's IPO is shaping up to be the ultimate Rorschach Test for the AI bull market.

Bulls see one of the most revolutionary companies in history, which, just five years after its founding, is leading the generative AI push, and whose Claude chatbot and related tools have become essential for millions of businesses and everyday users.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Bears, on the other hand, see a company writing checks that its chatbots can't cash. It has over $500 billion in future spending commitments and reported an $80.7 billion generally accepted accounting principles ( GAAP ) loss in the first half of the year, though that was mostly related to changes in valuations of its convertible debt due to the company's soaring valuation.

The bull vs. bear debate is about to get real once the AI stock goes public at an expected valuation of $2 trillion, but investors got a chunk of information to chew on from its S-1 prospectus out on Monday, and one of the noteworthy factoids was Anthropic's relationship with Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT).

Anthropic will pay Microsoft at least $45 billion

Microsoft was the last of the three big cloud computing platforms to invest in Anthropic, in part due to its close relationship with OpenAI, but the Windows parent is one of several cloud platforms Anthropic has contracted with for computing power.

According to the S-1, Anthropic will spend at least $44.9 billion between November 2026 and May 2033, regardless of its usage, and the agreement is mostly non-cancellable.

Anthropic has committed to spending $114.5 billion during a similar time frame with Alphabet , $110 billion with Amazon through 2036, and approximately $3.1 billion per month with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) through 2029.

That list is not exhaustive of its spending commitments and implies at least $400 billion in cloud infrastructure spending over the next several years.

What it means for Anthropic

Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on compute and infrastructure in the first half of the year, and that was its biggest line item cost by far.

The company's future cloud spending commitments go hand in hand with its growth. Computing power is what drives the business, and spending on it is as elemental as a restaurant spending on food.

The numbers may be eye-popping, and they do imply a lot of risks in the business if demand doesn't show up, but computing power is scarce right now, and Anthropic needs to make such moves to secure compute, or it will struggle to grow.

Story Continues

Investors scared off by such commitments may be better off taking the other side of the bet and investing in the cloud computing giants. Of course, those companies are spending hundreds of billions on building out those data centers to provide companies like Anthropic with the computing they need, and stocks like Microsoft are clearly less risky than AI start-ups like Anthropic.

The bull vs. bear debate will continue no matter what happens when Anthropic goes public, but the AI lab's debut will give investors a clear idea of where AI sentiment stands today. There's a lot of upside and downside to Anthropic stock, especially in the coming months.

Let's take a closer look at the 'Cloud Computing' theme and take a glance at a stock within, namely Microsoft MSFT.

Cloud Computing Overview

Cloud computing refers to the on-demand seamless access of computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence over the Internet (the cloud) on a pay-per-use pricing model.

It marks a paradigm shift from traditional on-premises infrastructure storage to remote cloud-based storage facilities and relies heavily on virtualization and automation technologies. Instead of buying, owning, and maintaining physical data centers and servers, organizations access a virtual pool of shared resources from a cloud service provider on an as-needed basis.

This lowers operating costs, increases productivity with greater agility and flexibility, and improves scalability with higher economies of scale.

Many have grown skeptical of the immense capital being thrown around in the broader AI frenzy, which helps explain some recent volatility we've seen among the broader tech sector. Investors are beginning to demand results from the investments for understandable reasons, driven by the lofty forecasts we've seen over the past several years.

Concerning consensus expectations for Microsoft's upcoming release, earnings are forecasted to grow 14% YoY on 16% higher revenues, maintaining an overall solid growth profile.

Thematic investing has emerged as a powerful way for investors to sync their portfolios with emerging trends. A mix of long-term and short-term themes is increasingly dictating which companies lead as economies expand and markets shift.

While stocks in each theme aren't direct recommendations, they offer a solid starting point. Leverage the Zacks Rank and other metrics to identify the best stocks for your strategy. Each featured stock comes with a Zacks report, giving you the tools to analyze performance and potential.

news.Title: Target has a problem that sends shoppers to Amazon
news.Content:
Target has always been my retail destination of choice, but I don't even have its app on my phone. That's because if I need something quickly, I go to Amazon.

If I need something only available from Target and I need it fast, I'll place my order on Uber Eats, even though it will often cost more than buying it in-store.

It's a weakness for the retail giant, as it's losing sales to Amazon and Walmart because those retailers offer next-day, and in some cases, same-day delivery.

That's an area where Target has been quietly investing in an effort to bridge the gap with its rivals.

Target improves its delivery

While Target has never been top-of-mind for me when it comes to delivery, the chain has been expanding its reach.

"Over 60% of the U.S. population has access to quicker, easier shopping as Target expands next-day delivery of online orders to more markets. Guests in more than 50 top U.S. metro areas will be able to get their purchases delivered next day — in many cases for free. It's yet another option among Target's fulfillment offerings, which also includes guest-favorite same-day services and two-day shipping," the chain shared in a press release .

Target owns Shipt , which offers free same-day delivery on orders over $35. It also offers a $99 annual membership that waives those limits.

More Target:

Target tackles a frustrating problem for shoppers

Target jumps on food trend Kroger and Publix embraced

Target rolls out another generous deal to win back customers

The chain has also expanded its selection of items available for delivery.

"Most items eligible for shipping at Target are eligible for next-day delivery. That includes hundreds of thousands of items — 85% of what we sell in Target stores," the chain shared.

Next-day delivery is free for orders over $35 or with no minimum order amount if you're a Target Circle 360 member or use your Target Circle Card for purchases.

"This is just one of the ways Target offers a convenient digital shopping experience. We already reach 80% of the U.S. population with same-day delivery — often within two or three hours — and 99% with two-day shipping. And our Order Pickup and Drive Up services are always free and available for guests on their timeline," Target shared.

Target needs to fix delivery

Target has a big bridge to cross in order to catch up to its rivals.

Walmart already serves nearly the entire country with same-day service.

"We expanded our U.S. store-fulfilled delivery areas in Q4 FY25. We can now reach 93% of U.S. households with same-day delivery," the company shared in its fourth-quarter 2025 earnings release .

Story Continues

That number climbed to 95%, according to an April press release .

eMarketer analyst Rachel Wolff warned in April that Target faces a difficult path to catching up with Amazon and Walmart on delivery speed.

"Target's delivery speed disadvantage underscores how difficult it is to catch up as Amazon and Walmart are zooming ahead. At this point, it's unclear whether Target has the means — or even the vision — to close the gaps with its competitors.

"Much of the company's turnaround strategy is rooted in returning to its pre-pandemic model, rather than reinventing the business for an age in which customer loyalty is more fragile and more spending is shifting online," she wrote.

Target tries to catch up to Amazon and Walmart

RTM Nexus CEO Dominick Miserandino had a simple response when I asked him about Target investing in delivery.

"They need to! They're the go to for that quick purchase and that feeling of getting it asap is the consumer standard," he told TheStreet.

Target COO Lisa Roath talked about delivery during the chain's second-quarter earnings call .

"We also saw meaningful gains in delivery speed. This past quarter, we fulfilled nearly 30% more same-day and next-day units than last year, and we will continue investing to get even faster," she said.

Delivery, she noted, is part of a broader effort to improve customer service.

"When we combine the impact of our in-store transitions, assortment changes, tech enhancements and improvements in inventory reliability, it all adds up to an elevated experience that is being noticed by our guests," she added.

Those efforts, Roath shared, have started to pay off.

"Overall satisfaction scores continue to improve across multiple measures of the guest experience, extending the momentum we shared with you last quarter and reinforcing that our continued investments in our teams, training and our team's tireless execution are making a difference," the COO said.

The chain has been addressing concerns that GlobalData Managing Director Neil Saunders raised in September ahead of Michael Fiddelke taking over as CEO.

"Visiting Target stores is less pleasurable and less fun than it used to be," Saunders said in an email. "There is far too much friction, and the experience is sometimes unpleasant. That's an issue as it lowers the probability of people making visits, reduces visit frequency, and weakens conversion and basket size when people are in stores," he told Retail Dive .

news.Title: Will Alphabet Stock Surge After Oct. 28?
news.Content:
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG)(NASDAQ: GOOGL) reports Q3 2026 earnings after the market closes on Oct. 28. Wall Street analysts have an average revenue estimate of $127.8 billion, which would be a 25% year-over-year increase, and earnings per share (EPS) of $3.

Last quarter, Alphabet easily surpassed revenue expectations -- and its share price still ended up falling 7% the next day. Based on the tech giant's recent track record, investors probably shouldn't feel too confident about which direction Alphabet stock will move immediately post-earnings.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What history says about Alphabet's post-earnings performance

The way Alphabet stock moves after an earnings report is about as predictable as a coin flip. Over the last four quarters, it has had an even split, closing higher the day after earnings twice and closing lower twice, despite beating headline EPS expectations each time. Its moves this year have been significant, closing up 10% after its April 29 report, and down 7.1% after its July 22 report.

Stretching it to the last 16 quarters, Alphabet has closed up seven times and closed down nine times. The average move is 5.2% in either direction.

Why July's beat turned into a sharp drop

Alphabet's earnings report in Q2 2026 looked great on the surface. Revenue was up 24% to $119.8 billion, Google Cloud revenue grew 82% to $24.8 billion, and EPS skyrocketed 294% to $9.11. The company's post-earnings slump makes more sense when you dig a little deeper.

Net income included about $99 billion in unrealized gains, mostly from Alphabet's investments in Space Exploration Technologies and Anthropic, and that caused the huge jump in EPS. These holdings are certainly valuable, but an increase in unrealized gains is much different from an increase in sales. Alphabet's adjusted EPS (without the unrealized gains) was $2.85, which actually missed consensus estimates by $0.04.

Alphabet also raised its 2026 capex guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion, and management said that 2027 capex will increase significantly. The company ended the quarter with negative free cash flow for the first time in its history since going public in 2004. The heavy spending worried investors and resulted in a sell-off.

What to watch on Oct. 28

Story Continues

There are a few potential swing factors, outside of revenue and EPS, to watch for in Alphabet's Q3 earnings. Any updates to its 2026 capex, as well as early guidance for 2027, could cause a big move, especially as rates have gone up and investors have become increasingly concerned with AI spending.

Free cash flow will give an idea of how manageable Alphabet's spending is. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said it will "remain under pressure" in the Q2 earnings call. How deep in the red it ends up will likely play a role in how the market reacts to earnings. Finally, Google Cloud revenue is a key metric, as it indicates that all the AI spending is turning into measurable sales growth. Ideally, Google Cloud growth will hold around 80%.

All that said, it's best to keep your expectations open. Earnings reports and post-earnings performance are inherently unpredictable. Considering how investors have rotated out of AI stocks recently, I think a decline in Alphabet stock is more likely than a surge post-earnings. However, when you're a long-term investor, what matters is what a company does over a period of years, not right after earnings.

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) gained 0.70% to 7,677, the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) rose 0.82% to 26,169 as AI optimism returned, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) edged up 0.28% to 52,362, diverging from Friday's energy-driven session as oil prices retreated.

Gold prices rose 0.46% to $4,026.30 as of U.S. market close and the 10-Year Treasury yield rose 0.04% to 5%, with investors favoring Real Estate and Technology stocks while Communication Services shares faced selling pressure.

Today's biggest moves

Surgery Partners (NASDAQ:SGRY) soared 48% on reports of a majority-stake takeover negotiation, while Lumentum (NASDAQ:LITE) jumped 8% following a bullish price target initiation. Conversely, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) fell 2% after filing to raise capital for AI infrastructure, and Petrobras (NYSE:PBR) plunged 14% following election results in Brazil.

What this means for investors

The big driver for Wall Street's tech stock rally on Oct. 26, 2026 was the long-awaited initial public offering (IPO) filing by artificial intelligence giant Anthropic. The company filed its S-1 prospectus to go public on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT." Its massive revenue growth figures in the filing calmed investor fears that the artificial intelligence boom was losing steam.

Anthropic's IPO revived enthusiasm for technology stocks, helping the Nasdaq Composite lead the market today despite pressure on more mature communication services providers. Adding to today's market performance was Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) stock gaining over 5%. Barclays upgraded shares to an Overweight rating, and raised its price target from $370 to $450 due to potential ties with CEO Elon Musk's other company, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), growth in Tesla's robotaxi business, and a recovery in its core automotive operations.

Meanwhile, Meta Platforms shares slipped after the company disclosed plans to raise up to $95 billion for AI infrastructure, signaling that the immense capital requirements for industry dominance remain a primary concern for mega-cap investors. Next, investors are looking ahead to this week's earnings from Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and the upcoming Federal Reserve interest rate decision, which will determine if the current momentum can survive tightening financial conditions.

news.Title: Don't Miss This Week's 5 Most Important Earnings Charts
news.Content:
Earnings season picks up steam this week with hundreds of S&P 500 companies reporting earnings including several of the Magnificent 7 stocks like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon.

The AI Revolution trade will also be in the spotlight with several key infrastructure companies reporting earnings.

But it's not just about technology this week. Big pharma, key restaurants like Wingstop, Chipotle and Starbucks, and big oil like ExxonMobil and Chevron will also report earnings.

True Earnings All-Stars

These are five of the top earnings charts this week. They are true earnings all-stars. These companies have excellent earnings surprise track records and some of the stocks are trading near all-time highs.

It's not easy to beat every quarter, or nearly every quarter, for several years in a row.

Can they beat again?

5 of the Most Important Earnings Charts This Week

1. Vertiv Holdings Co. ( VRT )

Vertiv has an excellent earnings surprise track record. It has only missed twice in the last 5 years and the last miss was in 2023.

Shares of Vertiv are down 21% over the last month as the AI trade has weakened. It's gotten more attractive on its valuation with a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of just 28.9.

With the bears in charge, will another beat even matter right now for Vertiv and the other AI stocks?

2. Microsoft Corp. ( MSFT )

Microsoft has an excellent earnings surprise record with just one miss in the last five years. That miss was all the way back in 2022.

Shares of Microsoft are up 3.2% in the last month, bucking the technology stock weakness. It's back to trading near its all-time highs.

Will Microsoft beat again this quarter?

3. Eli Lilly & Co. ( LLY )

Eli Lilly has strung together five earnings surprises in a row. The shares are up 8% in the last month and are trading near all-time highs.

Eli Lilly isn't cheap. It trades with a forward P/E of 38 but you are buying the earnings growth which is expected to be up 37% in 2026.

Is it too late to get into Eli Lilly?

4. Sandisk Corp. ( SNDK )

Sandisk is an earnings all-star. It hasn't missed on earnings since it was spun off from Western Digital in 2025.

Shares of Sandisk have fallen 29% over the last month on the fears over the AI slowdown. It is now dirt cheap. Sandisk trades with a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of just 5.8. A P/E ratio under 10 means a company is a deep value.

Will another Sandisk beat even matter for the stock?

5. Alphabet Inc. ( GOOGL )

Alphabet has an excellent earnings track record. It hasn't missed since the AI Revolution began in 2023.

Story Continues

Shares of Alphabet are down 7.8% in the last month. Alphabet is cheaper than every with a forward P/E of 15.6. That's near a historic low for the company.

Will Alphabet beat again this quarter?

news.Title: Trading Day: AI light, Brazil flight
news.Content:
By Jamie McGeever

ORLANDO, Florida, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Stocks mostly rose on Monday, lifted by renewed optimism around AI as Anthropic filed for a US IPO and as investors awaited more 'Big Tech' earnings later this week. Weaker oil prices also support risk appetite.

The big exception, however, was Brazil, where financial assets plunged ‌following left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's shock win in Sunday's presidential election.

In my column today, I look at whether 'stagflation' pressures may be building in the US. ‌A deflating artificial intelligence bubble puts downward pressure on Wall Street and wider economic growth, but the revival of oil and energy prices is putting upward pressure on inflation. It's a tricky one for investors, and the ​Fed.

Today's Key Reads

• Brazil stocks, real tumble as Lula win ends bullish run

• Anthropic's IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs

• Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion

• In China, the AI bubble has already burst

• Fed to hit pause on rate hikes, but maybe not for long

• Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: Brazil -14%. Asia mixed, Europe and UK up around 0.8%. Wall Street higher: Nasdaq +0.8%, S&P 500 +0.7%, Dow +0.3%.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Tech +1.5%, comms services -1.4%. Tesla +5%, DoorDash -6%.FX: Brazilian real -8.5%, biggest fall since devaluation in 1999. Philippine peso sinks ‌to record low near 64.00/$. US dollar index edges higher.BONDS: ⁠Brazil buys back bonds, cancels auctions. US 2-year auction is ok — foreign demand dips, domestic demand surges.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil slips — Brent -0.8%, WTI -1.5%. Gold +0.5% back above $4,000/oz.

Today's Talking Points:

AI funding blitz

If investors were showing signs of AI fatigue in recent weeks, they're hiding it well as this week gets underway. On Monday, ⁠Anthropic filed for a US IPO, Meta announced plans for a $95 billion equity raise, and SpaceX said it has struck a $40 billion deal with Apollo Global Management for AI chip funding. The Anthropic IPO could value the company at a record-breaking $1.5 trillion or more, and Meta's capital raise would also be a record.

The eye-popping sums needed to fund the AI buildout have begun to suck some of the ​air ​out of the AI bubble, but that was shrugged off on Monday, at least temporarily — tech and AI ​stocks fueled a solid rebound on Wall Street. Competition for investor ‌capital is heating up.

Brazil

Politically, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise election victory on Sunday was truly historic: never before had a candidate won the decisive second-round vote after losing the first. It also means a record-setting fourth term for Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday. Unsurprisingly, given the historic significance of Lula's comeback, there was a reaction across Brazilian markets.

Story Continues

Few doubt the scale of Brazil's fiscal and economic challenges, but Monday's collapse in Brazilian assets is likely to reverse, to some degree. Part of the selloff was because investors were caught so flat-footed. As late as Sunday, prediction markets were pointing to an 80% chance of a win for Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. But Lula's scope to push through an agenda that investors fear will ‌be limited, due to Bolsonaro's backing in Congress.

Central bank bonanza

This week is one of the busiest in years ​for policymaking in the world's developed economies, with half of the G10 central banks set to decide interest ​rates. Monetary authorities in New Zealand and Canada are widely expected to hike by ​25 basis points, while those in the US, euro zone and Japan are expected to keep them on hold but signal possible increases in ‌December.

The common enemy is inflation, which is already too sticky in many ​countries. Oil and global energy prices remain elevated ​as war continues to choke Middle East supply routes, and the worry for policymakers is this bleeds into core inflation and becomes embedded in inflation expectations. But if the AI bubble deflates, growth, consumer confidence and investor sentiment could deflate too, putting policymakers in an even tighter bind.

What could move markets tomorrow?

• Japan services producer price inflation (September)

• ​South Korea GDP (Q3, advance)

• US Treasury sells $70 billion of 5-year notes ‌at auction

• US durable goods (September)

• Corporate earnings, including Visa, Coca-Cola, Boeing, Seagate Technology, HSBC, Novartis

news.Title: Why Google might avoid an earnings 'reckoning' this week
news.Content:
Google's ( GOOG ) investors have a few things in their favor coming into earnings day this week that Meta ( META ) investors weren't afforded when the tech giant reported a few negative surprises .

"Google has already done some of its fundraising and indicated a 'significant' increase in capex next year when it reported Q2, so that particular reckoning may be behind it," D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria wrote in a note on Monday. "It is worth noting that Mr. Brin and Mr. Page moved out of California before the 1/1/26 cutoff and may be able to avoid having to sell their shares. Which means that investors will be able to focus on the Anthropic-driven growth in Google Cloud."

Meta surprised investors last week on several fronts.

The company posted negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive AI spending. It signaled more aggressive spending in coming quarters.

To fund that spending, it further surprised investors by establishing a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock, which effectively serves as a 2-for-1 stock split.

Under the scheme — in part designed to keep founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg working in California as the 5% billionaire's tax looms — existing shareholders will receive one new nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they hold. Trading is slated to begin in January 2027.

Issuing nonvoting stock allows Zuckerberg to raise external capital for Meta's AI build-out without diluting his personal voting control over the tech giant.

Meta shares have come under pressure on fears Zuckerberg may have to sell shares to pay for his Prop 40 tax bill.

But as Luria pointed out, Google investors need not worry on this front.

Co-founder Larry Page bought two Miami estates for a combined $173.4 million, the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year. His co-founder, Sergey Brin, moved to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe and also bought a home in Miami this year, Fortune reported.

"We expect the company to discuss its plans to regain primacy in AI, where it is now a 2nd or 3rd place in each of the markets — 2nd in chat to ChatGPT, 3rd in enterprise to Anthropic and OpenAI, and now even trailing Meta's Muse in the personal AI assistant market," Luria wrote about Google's upcoming earnings report.

news.Title: Tesla Isn’t a Hyperscaler. Why the AI Bears Are Misreading Its $5 Billion Capex Cut.
news.Content:
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) is spending less money than originally planned this year. And for investors who track how much money is being poured into artificial intelligence, that might sound like bad news.

But Tesla's decision to reduce its 2026 capital expenditure (capex) forecast by more than $5 billion isn't necessarily a warning about AI demand. In fact, it could be a smart move for the electric vehicle maker.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The reason is simple. Tesla doesn't need to build massive amounts of computing capacity to compete with Amazon , Alphabet , and Microsoft .

That's not its business.

Image source: Tesla.

Tesla is still all-in on AI

On Tesla's third-quarter earnings call , Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja announced the company reduced its 2026 capex forecast from more than $25 billion to approximately $20 billion.

The reduction doesn't mean Tesla is backing away from artificial intelligence. The company continues to develop its Full Self-Driving technology, expand its Cybercab robotaxi program , and work on its Optimus humanoid robots. All three projects require considerable investment. But they don't require Tesla to build the equivalent of Amazon Web Services or Microsoft's Azure.

Tesla needs computing power to train its AI models and improve its autonomous systems. It also needs manufacturing capacity to produce vehicles and robots, as well as the infrastructure to operate its planned robotaxi fleet.

Those investments serve a specific purpose: developing products and services Tesla can eventually sell to customers.

Tesla doesn't need to win the data center race

Cloud computing companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars building data centers to support AI workloads. Alphabet raised its 2026 capex forecast to $200 billion, while Amazon increased its spending plans to $220 billion.

The aggressive spending makes a lot of sense. Those companies are building computing infrastructure that supports their existing cloud businesses, serves external customers, and provides the capacity needed to meet growing demand for AI services. Tesla has a different business model.

That doesn't mean Elon Musk's company can stop investing in AI infrastructure. Training autonomous driving models requires enormous computing resources, and those requirements could increase as the company expands its ambitions.

Story Continues

But there's little reason for Tesla to match the spending of companies whose business is selling computing capacity. In fact, building more infrastructure than it needs would tie up capital that could be used to expand vehicle production, develop Optimus, or support its robotaxi business.

And with those businesses still developing, Tesla has good reasons to be selective about where its money goes.

Tesla's capex cut is good news for investors

Tesla posted $28.05 billion in revenue for the third quarter, essentially unchanged from a year earlier. Automotive revenue declined 3%, while operating margins narrowed from 5.8% to 2.6%. Those numbers demonstrate that Tesla can't rely on its automotive business to generate unlimited amounts of cash for new projects.

But even so, Tesla generated $1.53 billion in free cash flow during the quarter and ended September with more than $45 billion in cash and investments. Cutting back on unneeded spending will give Tesla more flexibility to work on its autonomous driving and robotics businesses.

And importantly, management hasn't suggested that its AI development plans are being scaled back. Taneja said capital spending is expected to increase in the coming years as Tesla expands robotaxi operations, Optimus manufacturing, and AI computing infrastructure.

So the reduction in this year's budget appears to be more about when Tesla spends money than whether it intends to make those investments.

For investors in Nvidia and other AI infrastructure suppliers, Tesla's decision also shouldn't be confused with a slowdown in hyperscaler spending. The companies building cloud computing infrastructure have different customers, different revenue opportunities, and much larger capital budgets.

Tesla's challenge isn't to build the world's biggest collection of data centers. It's to turn AI technology into profitable products. And if the company can accomplish that while spending $5 billion less than originally planned, shareholders have every reason to welcome the decision.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

news.Title: Tesla stock leaves rest of the Magnificent 7 in the dust, surging to October's top spot
news.Content:
For most of 2026, Tesla has been the Magnificent Seven's minivan. In October, it's the only one leaving skid marks.

Tesla ( TSLA ) stock jumped about 5% Monday, its best day since early September and its highest close in about three months. The rest of Big Tech was a mixed bag, with Apple ( AAPL ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ) all ending lower.

That leaves Tesla with two very different report cards. It's still down by double digits this year, the worst showing in the Magnificent Seven. But it's up by double digits in October, the best in the group, while Meta, Alphabet, and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are all lower for the month.

Tesla is breaking through a crowded spot on the chart

The stock opened above Friday's high — a gap — and pushed through the $386 area. That level is both Tesla's highest close of October and roughly its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line many traders watch. Clearing both at once is what makes this a breakout.

Even so, Tesla remains about a fifth below its record close.

The SpaceX connection

The rally came alongside a Barclays upgrade betting that a Tesla merger with SpaceX ( SPCX ) would hand shareholders a takeout premium , as Pras Subramanian reported . Barclays raised its price target to $450 from $370. Musk confirmed last week that the two companies had formed independent committees to explore a combination, though no deal has been announced.

Tesla is already in on the joke. On Monday, its Robotaxi service switched on a bigger Houston service area shaped like a Starship rocket, announced with a "Houston, we have liftoff" post. "I swear it's just a coincidence 😂," Musk replied on X.

A combination wouldn't just bring rockets. On Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy AI chips, and he also warned about neoclouds — rent-a-GPU cloud companies such as CoreWeave ( CRWV ) — as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . A merged company would share that chip bill.

Watch $386. Holding it keeps the liftoff on course, while a slide back below would turn Monday into a one-day pop. Above, the next stop is the low $450s, where Barclays' target and Tesla's 2026 closing high nearly overlap.

news.Content:
Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results on deck from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).

Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.

It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.

Inflationary environment drives softer quarter for Whirlpool

Whirlpool posted another mixed quarter as inflation and lower demand in North America took a toll.

Revenue for major appliances in its North America business fell 8.3% year over year to $2.5 billion, below Wall Street's expectations.

news.Title: Anthropic's IPO Keeps Founders in Control Through a "Founder LLC" Voting Structure
news.Content:
The initial public offering (IPO) queue just welcomed its most unconventional corporate creature yet. Artificial intelligence (AI) heavyweight Anthropic, the developer behind the Claude platform, officially filed its Form S-1 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) today.

The filing sets the stage for a Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT. But beneath Anthropic's staggering compute numbers and explosive top-line growth lies a governance framework that should stop prospective shareholders in their tracks.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Silicon Valley has long treated public investors as passive passengers. Mega-cap innovators like Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) built modern market empires on dual- or triple-class equities. Their stock structures grant public buyers economic claims while effectively walling off boardroom power behind insider shares.

But Anthropic's proposed setup makes even those founder-friendly bastions look tame. Instead of merely weighting voting rights based on who owns the most stock, Anthropic is slicing ownership, shareholder voting, and board oversight into five distinct share classes.

Anthropic Share Class

Number of Shares

Economic Rights

Voting Power

Class A

Up to 300 billion shares

Standard

1 vote per share

Class E

Up to 30 billion shares

None

1 vote per share (special matters only)

Class F

50.1% of the total power in ordinary shareholder votes

Class N

Up to 100 billion shares

Class T

1 vote per share (Board elections only)

Data from Anthropic's S-1 filing.

The 4 Major Differences

1. A single "golden share" instead of billions of shares (Class F)

SpaceX and Meta are the same story. Musk and Zuckerberg both have total control over shareholder votes through their massive holdings of supervoting Class B shares. They have the option to convert these shares into common stock if they want to raise personal cash, but then they would gradually lose their voting power.

At Anthropic, the founders created Class F common stock consisting of a single share held by the founders' LLC. It has no economic rights (no claim to profits or dividends) but gives the co-founders 50.1% of the total vote on all general corporate matters. The vote counts of other classes don't even matter in most cases; Class F decides the outcome of simple-majority votes.

Story Continues

Class E is another voting-only stock, but holds no sway in ordinary shareholder votes. Instead, its holders control the structure of the Long Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), the Public Benefit Corporation (PBC) status, and changes to Anthropic's Charter. It's a safeguard against Class F holders restructuring the company at will.

2. The board has an outside "safety valve" (Class T & the trust)

Elon Musk is on the board of SpaceX. It's a controlled company, and the board reports directly to him on a supermajority basis.

At Anthropic, the LTBT is an independent body of AI safety, national security, and policy experts holding the Class T shares. Shares in this class have no financial claim but have the sole right to elect and remove a majority of the Board of Directors. The founders hold 50.1% of general shareholder voting power via Class F shares but cannot outvote or remove the board majority elected by the Trust.

3. Strategic cloud partners are boxed out of governance (Class N)

Big tech investors such as Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet invested billions in Anthropic over the years. To prevent major partners from gaining control of the board or triggering antitrust and regulatory issues, Anthropic created Class N common stock. Class N shares have full financial ownership but no voting rights.

4. Fiduciary duty: "Mission" over shareholder value (PBC status)

Meta and Alphabet are conventional corporations registered in Delaware, whose boards have a general fiduciary duty to create value for equity shareholders. SpaceX moved its registration to Texas in 2024.

Anthropic is registered in Delaware, but as a PBC. By charter, the board must balance financial return against the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." If the Trust determines commercial profit conflicts with safe deployment, the Trust-controlled board can legally prioritize safety over stock returns.

Remember, the Trust holds Class T shares and can replace the Board of Directors if needed. That's real power.

The Bottom Line

Alphabet pioneered non-voting Class C stock to fund equity compensation without diluting its founders' majority control. Meta has adopted a similar blueprint, creating Class C shares to finance $140B in AI infrastructure and personal tax liabilities while permanently locking Mark Zuckerberg's 61% voting majority against outside dilution. And at SpaceX, Musk has total control as his high number of supervotes completely dominates the boardroom.

In Anthropic's proposed structure, the founders have 50.1% of operational votes via an empty economic shell (Class F) and have effectively handed ultimate board control to an independent safety trust (Class T). Public investors buying Class A get financial exposure to the business, but governance is forever in the hands of Class F and Class T holders.

At Anthropic, Wall Street gets to pick up the tab for the compute bills, but it will never get a seat at the table. Make sure you're OK with this structure before buying Anthropic shares.

news.Content:
Microsoft on Monday announced a new voluntary buyout program that will cover about 60,000 eligible employees who can choose to leave the company with financial support and other career planning resources.

The buyout program covers more than a quarter of Microsoft's global workforce, as the company said it had about 223,000 full-time employees around the world as of June 30, 2026, in its annual filing. The voluntary exit program was first reported by Business Insider and follows Microsoft's rollout of a voluntary retirement program earlier this year.

Amy Coleman, Microsoft EVP and chief people officer, said in a memo posted on the official Microsoft blog that the buyout program "reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter."

The company's voluntary exit program is time-limited and available to eligible employees at level 70 and below. Microsoft's announcement indicated that eligible employees would be notified via email about the details of their voluntary exit offer within a few hours of the announcement.

Coleman added that the voluntary exit offer is new to Microsoft and that the company will learn from it and added, "At the same time, we'll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft."

Microsoft Ceo Says Superintelligence Must Remain 'Under Human Control'

news.Title: AI Headlines Pile Up as Wall Street Navigates a Volatile Week
news.Content:
Things are happening, folks.

Anthropic officially filed for its IPO this morning, SpaceX secured $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs, Meta announced plans for a $95 billion equity offering, and concerns surrounding the neocloud industry continue to intensify.

And that's just the AI news.

We also have five major central banks meeting this week, including the Federal Reserve on Wednesday, followed by GDP and PCE inflation data on Thursday. Meanwhile, roughly 25% of the S&P 500 by market capitalization is set to report earnings, including three of the largest AI hyperscalers, the oil majors and several major pharmaceutical companies.

All of this comes as the major indexes are navigating elevated volatility, trading near the lower end of their recent ranges as the midterm elections approach and geopolitical tensions continue to rise.

There is a lot to cover, so let's get into it.

Image Source: TradingView

Anthropic Opens Its Books: The First Look at Frontier AI Economics

One of the biggest developments this morning was Anthropic's public S-1 filing, officially setting the stage for its initial public offering later this year. The company, best known for its Claude family of AI models, plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

The short version is that the numbers are quite good. Really, they're extraordinary.

Revenue increased from just $41 million in 2023 to $386 million in 2024, before surging to approximately $4.6 billion in 2025. In the first six months of 2026 alone, revenue reached $16.3 billion, roughly 14 times the level generated during the same period last year.

Of course, the company is spending enormous sums to support that growth, but the underlying business economics appear considerably more compelling than many had anticipated.

Anthropic reported a $693 million operating loss during the first half of 2026, narrowing sharply from $2.1 billion in the prior-year period. Gross margins are also reportedly approaching 85%, suggesting an increasingly attractive revenue model as the business scales.

There was also a staggering $80.7 billion net loss, but that figure is somewhat misleading. Roughly $72.4 billion came from a noncash accounting adjustment required to revalue outstanding convertible notes as Anthropic's valuation surged.

Meanwhile, the company reported an enormous $112.4 billion cash reserve as of June 30, alongside another $19.3 billion in short-term investments.

This was all better than I had expected.

For several years, one of the biggest uncertainties hanging over the AI trade has been the lack of visibility into the economics of the companies actually developing these frontier models.

Story Continues

We have been able to see the enormous revenues flowing to Nvidia, the semiconductor manufacturers and infrastructure providers, but had very little insight into whether their customers were building sustainable businesses.

Now, for the first time, we have a detailed look at one of the leading AI developers, and the initial picture is encouraging.

There are still plenty of questions about future computing obligations, operating expenses and long-term profitability. But Anthropic's extraordinary revenue growth, improving operating results and substantial liquidity suggest the commercial opportunity is very real.

And as more of these businesses move toward public ownership, the additional transparency could remove a meaningful source of uncertainty surrounding the entire AI investment cycle.

SpaceX Raises $40 Billion While Neoclouds Struggle

SpaceX (SPCX) announced over the weekend that it had secured approximately $40 billion in debt financing to purchase AI chips, highlighting the extraordinary scale of investment still flowing into the industry.

The announcement follows SpaceX's third-quarter earnings report last week, which revealed an explosion in AI-related revenue that increasingly complements its established Starlink and rocket-launch businesses.

Of the approximately $14.6 billion in quarterly revenue, $7.56 billion came from its AI business, which expanded nearly tenfold year over year.

That diversification is becoming an increasingly important advantage.

Musk also had some interesting comments on X regarding AI infrastructure financing and the neocloud industry.

According to Musk, debt markets have become far less willing to lend to businesses without substantial revenue streams outside AI data centers. He argued that SpaceX was able to secure financing because of its investment-grade balance sheet and established Starlink and launch revenues.

He also predicted substantial failures and consolidation among the more than 200 neocloud operators, describing the coming shakeout as "guppy-level death and consolidation."

Those are pretty stark comments, but the market has already been signaling growing concerns about the industry's financial sustainability.

For those unfamiliar, neoclouds are specialized cloud computing businesses that build data centers and rent computing capacity to AI developers and enterprise customers.

Companies such as CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and IREN (IREN) have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom, but their expansion strategies require enormous amounts of capital, much of it financed through debt.

As interest rates have risen and lenders have become more concerned about the durability of these business models, the sustainability of that approach has come into question.

CoreWeave has been at the center of the turmoil.

Some of the company's unsecured bonds have fallen below 80 cents on the dollar, levels typically associated with distressed debt, while yields on certain issues have climbed above 15%.

That is a significant warning sign.

A company whose business model depends on continuously borrowing billions of dollars to expand computing capacity faces a much more difficult environment when lenders suddenly demand substantially higher returns.

CoreWeave and other neocloud operators have substantial contracted revenue backlogs, and demand for computing capacity remains extremely strong. That is the bullish side of the argument.

But strong demand does not necessarily guarantee a sustainable business model, particularly when financing costs, equipment depreciation and future capital requirements are all moving targets.

I continue to believe the AI infrastructure boom has considerable room to run, but the market is increasingly distinguishing between companies with strong balance sheets and established cash flows and those dependent on continued access to external capital.

That distinction could become one of the defining themes of the next phase of the AI investment cycle.

Meta Turns to Equity Markets to Finance Its AI Expansion

Also this morning, Meta Platforms (META) announced plans to raise as much as $95 billion through equity issuance to help finance its enormous AI expansion.

The announcement follows last week's earnings report, when Meta beat estimates on both the top and bottom lines and raised its expected 2026 capital expenditures to between $135 billion and $145 billion.

That is an extraordinary amount of money, even for a company of Meta's size.

The financing plan begins with approximately $35 billion in common and preferred stock offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion that could be raised through an at-the-market equity program next year.

What makes this development particularly interesting is the change in how Meta is financing its investments.

Until recently, the company had largely funded its capital expenditures through the enormous cash flows generated by its advertising business. Now, it is turning directly to shareholders for additional capital.

It is also a different approach from SpaceX, which has relied heavily on debt financing.

And Meta is not alone.

Alphabet (GOOGL) completed a similar $90 billion multi-tranche equity and equity-linked capital-raising program in June, including common equity, convertible preferred shares, a private placement and an at-the-market offering.

We are now seeing some of the largest and most profitable companies in the world turn to external financing to support their AI ambitions.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that. In fact, issuing equity can be a more conservative approach than taking on excessive debt, particularly when the returns on these investments remain uncertain.

But it does introduce dilution risk for existing shareholders, and it illustrates just how much capital the AI industry is consuming.

Another interesting detail is that Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have reportedly expressed interest in purchasing up to $5 billion of Meta's offering collectively.

In other words, some of the companies supplying AI infrastructure are now potentially helping finance the customers buying their products.

Taken together, these announcements highlight an important evolution in the AI investment cycle.

For the last several years, the primary focus has been on how quickly companies can build out computing infrastructure. Increasingly, the questions are shifting toward how that expansion will be financed, what the capital will cost and whether the eventual returns will justify the investment.

The demand side of the equation still looks exceptionally strong. But financing is becoming an increasingly important consideration, and the market is beginning to take notice.

Five Central Banks, Three Days and Another Critical Fed Decision

Beyond the AI headlines, the macroeconomic calendar is exceptionally busy this week.

Five major central banks are scheduled to announce interest rate decisions over the next three days, including the Federal Reserve, Bank of Canada, Reserve Bank of New Zealand, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.

The general expectation is for most policymakers to leave rates unchanged, although New Zealand and Canada could potentially deliver additional hikes.

In the United States, the Federal Reserve is widely expected to hold its benchmark policy rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, with fed funds futures pricing approximately an 89.5% probability of no change as of this writing.

That makes the decision itself somewhat less important than the accompanying commentary from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, although he has generally been reluctant to offer much in the way of explicit forward guidance.

The more important question is whether the Fed sees enough evidence of persistent inflation to justify another rate hike before year-end.

Recent economic resilience, rising energy prices and stubborn inflation pressures have complicated the outlook considerably.

And given the growing concerns surrounding debt-financed AI expansion, the direction of interest rates is becoming even more consequential for the technology sector.

We also have two important economic releases on Thursday morning, with the advance estimate for third-quarter GDP and the September Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation report.

The GDP report should offer another useful indication of the economy's underlying momentum, while PCE remains one of the Fed's preferred measures of inflation.

A hotter-than-expected inflation print immediately following Wednesday's Fed decision could quickly shift expectations for December and put additional pressure on the bond market.

With interest rates already elevated and financial conditions becoming more restrictive, these releases have the potential to generate meaningful volatility across asset classes.

Big Tech Earnings Take Center Stage

Finally, we have another exceptionally important week of corporate earnings.

The third-quarter reporting season is moving into full swing, with more than 130 S&P 500 companies expected to release results over the coming days.

Several of the world's largest technology companies will be reporting, including Alphabet, Microsoft (MSFT) and Amazon (AMZN).

Of course, investors will be watching the traditional metrics, including cloud revenue growth, operating margins, earnings guidance and the performance of each company's core businesses.

But I suspect the biggest questions will center around capital expenditures.

How much more are these companies planning to spend on AI infrastructure? Are they beginning to see meaningful returns from their investments? And perhaps most importantly, how much additional financing will they need to support their expansion plans?

After the developments at Meta, SpaceX and across the neocloud industry, those questions are likely to receive considerably more attention.

The hyperscalers have been the primary drivers of the enormous capital investment cycle supporting semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators, power infrastructure providers and countless other businesses.

As long as that spending continues to grow, it should remain a powerful tailwind for the broader AI ecosystem.

However, any suggestion that these companies are becoming more cautious could create another round of volatility, particularly among the more speculative infrastructure providers.

Outside technology, we also have major earnings reports from Eli Lilly (LLY), Mastercard (MA), Exxon Mobil (XOM) and Chevron (CVX), among many others.

Energy and technology have been major contributors to S&P 500 earnings growth, making these reports particularly important for assessing the strength of corporate profits.

I'll also be watching for continued signs of earnings growth broadening beyond the technology sector, which would be an encouraging development for the sustainability of the bull market.

What to Expect in the Stock Market This Week

There is a lot for investors to digest this week, and given the recent volatility, I wouldn't be surprised to see some sharp market reactions to the incoming headlines.

My broader outlook remains constructive. The AI infrastructure boom, substantial fiscal spending and relatively abundant liquidity continue to provide important support for economic activity and corporate earnings.

However, the latest financing developments are worth taking seriously.

The scale of capital investment is becoming extraordinary, borrowing costs are rising, and investors are beginning to distinguish more carefully between companies with sustainable cash flows and those heavily dependent on external financing.

I don't see these developments as evidence that the AI boom is ending. Rather, they suggest the investment cycle is entering a more mature and potentially more selective phase.

And despite the recent selling, there is still plenty of evidence that underlying demand remains exceptionally strong. Anthropic's financial disclosures were a particularly encouraging development on that front.

With central bank decisions, major economic reports and hyperscaler earnings all arriving over the next few days, we should have a much clearer picture of where the market stands by the end of the week.

For now, I think patience and selectivity remain important. We could certainly see additional volatility as the midterm elections approach, but I continue to believe the underlying bull-market drivers are intact.

And if those fundamentals continue to hold up, the recent selling could ultimately create some very attractive opportunities.

Understanding the Neocloud Debt Concerns

Until recently, Neoclouds, specialized cloud computing providers built specifically for artificial intelligence, have been among the best-performing stocks on Wall Street. However, over the past few weeks, investors in Neocloud stocks such as Nebius Group ( NBIS ), IREN ( IREN ), and CoreWeave ( CRWV ) have endured immense selling pressure and volatility amid rising debt concerns.

What Caused Neocloud Stocks to Plunge?

On October 14th, CoreWeave shares fell more than 15% as bond yields jumped to distressed levels and Gartner warned of potential for slowdowns in AI infrastructure spending. After the initial pressure, a second wave hit after Meta Platforms ( META ) reported its first negative free cash flow quarter as a public company, sparking Wall Street concerns about the growing mismatch between massive Capex spending and cash flow.

Musk Sounds the Alarm on Neocloud Stocks

Over the weekend, Elon Musk sounded the alarm on pure-play Neocloud companies, saying:

"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers. SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we're investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue. That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through but not many."

News Failure: Neoclouds Rally Despite Musk Warning

Seasoned investors know that monitoring price action relative to the news is more valuable than monitoring the news alone. Historically, stocks bottom on bad news. For example, on March 18th, 2020, billionaire investor Bill Ackman appeared on financial news TV and warned that "Hell is coming!" due to COVID-19 lockdowns. Three days later, the stock market bottomed and never looked back.

Image Source: TradingView

Monday's action in Neocloud stocks eerily mirrors Bill Ackman's warning during COVID. Most investors would assume Neoclouds would plunge further after Elon Musk's dire warning. However, on Monday, Neocloud stocks delivered a classic expectation breaker, ripping from red to green, and setting the stage for a potential bottom.

Bottom Line

While tighter debt markets and heavy capital expenditures pose a real hurdle for pure-play Neoclouds, market history suggests the worst fears may already be priced in. The surprising resilience of Neocloud shares after high-profile warnings mirrors past market bottoms, when asset prices reversed course just as headlines seemed most dire.

The Legal Hit and What It Means

The New Mexico judge ordered a fine of $25 billion from Meta after a jury ruled the company broke the state Consumer Protection Act in the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Meta is appealing the penalty, saying it's unconstitutional and that it'll likely be thrown out in appeals court.

It's quite a judgment, though it could be more or less impactful based on the appeals path taken. Investors' sentiment has been dampened by broader privacy and child-safety legal liability on top of the settlement previously agreed by Meta to settle a lawsuit filed by a multistate coalition against Cambridge Analytica.

The big question now is how many other states will follow suit and add to Meta's legal expenses? The company had ample liquidity, with $44.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents, to buffer it against a financial storm.

And the ruling on its own does not destroy the foundational ads business for Meta. So despite the high cost, this isn't a serious threat to its ads business. However, the key thing investors need to watch out for is if these growing legal fees become a priority over business performance.

Meta's Latest Earnings Show a Business Is Booming

Meta delivered a strong third quarter, with revenue and adjusted earnings beating Wall Street expectations.

Revenue climbed 26% year-over-year (YoY) to $64.6 billion, topping analysts' consensus estimate of $63.37 billion. Advertising remained the company's biggest growth engine, with sales rising 26% to $63.1 billion.

However, profit was hit due to some ongoing legal issues. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $7.40, well above the $5.75 analysts had expected. However, Meta reported net income of $9.9 billion after recording a $9.9 billion legal settlement charge.

The bigger concern was cash flow. Free cash flow turned negative at $2.1 billion, marking Meta's first negative quarterly reading since its 2012 IPO. Capital expenditures jumped 80% to nearly $35 billion, and management raised the lower end of its full-year spending outlook, now expecting capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion.

Meta is pouring billions into AI infrastructure, betting that the investment will fuel future growth. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, pointing to annual growth of 22% to 27%.

For investors, it's not clear. While the advertising business is still robust, the costs of artificial intelligence and the business's faltering cash flow pose the question of how much the company will need to spend before those investments start paying off.

The Muse AI Story Is Real

Meta introduced its AI agents under the name of "Muse" in September. Muse has already been used by more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada. Approximately 25% of users interact with it every day. If that's the case, then Zuckerberg claims Muse will be able to earn more money per user than the entire Family of Apps.

The firm also said it'll carry out a two-for-one split of its stock using a new class of non-voting shares. The stock is to be distributed in the first of 2027. This doesn't alter the stock's true value but will result in a more attractive stock price and provide discounted liquidity for acquisitions and payroll to META stock.

Analysts See Major Upside for META Stock

Despite all of these worrying signs, Wall Street is not blinking. The consensus rating is still a solid "Strong Buy." The 12-month average price target sits at $855.67, implying 34% upside from here.

Separately, Goldman Sachs has a "Buy" rating and raises its price target to $885. Analyst Eric Sheridan says the risk-reward skew remains positive. "We still see a positive risk/reward skew on current shares when measured against the core business operating momentum," he wrote.

JPMorgan is even more bullish. Doug Anmuth raised his target to $940. He calls this the first quarter where Meta's "superintelligence" vision met "early product momentum."

Morgan Stanley keeps an "Overweight" rating and an $820 target. The firm calls Meta the "cleanest consumer GenAI winner." Barclays raised its target to $880. Analyst Ross Sandler says, "Muse is off to a great start and represents a game changer for the META narrative."

Meta trades at a forward P/E of 19 based on 2027 estimates. The sector median is closer to 28. That looks cheap for a company growing revenue north of 20%. The legal bill is huge. The AI spending is huge. But the core ad machine is still humming.

From my perspective, Investors with a long horizon should see this dip as an opportunity, not a trap.

What to Expect From Q3 Earnings
